paragraphs: Let us examine whether this position is just. It will be granted, I think, that no state has so far existed, at least none of which we have any record, where manners were so pure and simple and the means of subsistence so abundant that nothing whatever checked early marriage. Among the lower classes there has been the fear of not providing well for a family. Among the higher classes there has been the fear of lowering their condition in life. Consequently, in no state we have known has the power of population been left to exert itself with perfect freedom.

Whether or not a law of marriage is established, the dictate of nature and virtue seems to be an early attachment to one woman. Even supposing a liberty to change partners after an unfortunate choice, this liberty would not affect population until it rose to a level of serious vice. And we are now supposing a society in which vice is scarcely known.

In a state of great equality and virtue, therefore, where pure and simple manners prevailed and subsistence was so abundant that nobody feared being unable to provide amply for a family, the power of population would act unchecked. The resulting increase of the human species would evidently be far greater than any increase so far known.

In the United States of America, the means of subsistence have been more ample and the manners of the people purer than in any modern European state. Consequently, the checks to early marriage have been fewer, and the population has been found to double itself in twenty-five years.

This rate falls short of the utmost power of population. Yet because it is the result of actual experience, we will take it as our rule. We will say that population, when unchecked, doubles itself every twenty-five years, or increases in a geometrical ratio.

Let us now take any spot of earth, this Island for instance, and see at what rate the subsistence it provides could be supposed to increase. We will begin with the Island in its present state of cultivation.

Suppose that, through the best possible policy, by breaking up more land and by greatly encouraging agriculture, the produce of this Island could be doubled in the first twenty-five years. That, I think, would be allowing as much as anyone could reasonably demand.

In the following twenty-five years, it is impossible to suppose that the produce could be quadrupled, since this would contradict all our knowledge of the qualities of land. The very most we can conceive is that the increase in the second twenty-five years might equal the present produce. Let us take this as our rule, though it is certainly far beyond the truth. Let us allow that, by great exertion, the whole produce of the Island might grow every twenty-five years by a quantity equal to what it now produces. Not even the most enthusiastic speculator can suppose a greater increase than this. Within a few centuries, it would make every acre of the Island like a garden.
